name: GAO on AI in Federal Government: Audits, Inventories and Guidance
title: GAO on AI in Federal Government: Audits, Inventories and Guidance
answer: The U.S. Government Accountability Office publishes audits, technology assessments and spotlights on how federal agencies use artificial intelligence. Its most useful contribution is the primary public record of that use: a review finding that 20 of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, most still in planning, with only about 200 in current use and many inventories incomplete.

sections.body: The Government Accountability Office, the audit and evaluation arm of the U.S. Congress, publishes reports, technology assessments and Science and Tech Spotlights on artificial intelligence across the federal government. The pages read span reports from 2020 through 2025, including a review of agency AI inventories, a spotlight on generative AI, a technology assessment of generative AI's environmental and human effects, a report on machine learning in natural hazard forecasting, and testimony describing GAO's own internal AI use. The material is public, non-commercial and addressed to policymakers including Congress, federal agencies, state and local governments, academia and industry.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The central document is GAO's review of federal AI reporting. Twenty of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three reported none. Reported uses included analyzing camera and radar data to identify border activities, analyzing drone photographs, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the most use cases. Most were still in planning, with roughly 200 in current use. Only five agencies provided comprehensive information for every use case, and 15 had incomplete or inaccurate data, with some inventories missing required elements such as life cycle stage or releasability, and two listing uses later determined not to be AI. On policy, the Office of Management and Budget had not developed acquisition and use guidance, the Office of Personnel Management had not established an AI occupational category, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy had not communicated which agencies were expected to meet specific requirements. Ten of 23 agencies implemented all agency-specific AI requirements, 12 implemented some and one was exempt. Separately, GAO's generative AI spotlight explains that these systems create text, images, audio and video from patterns in massive datasets, can hallucinate credible-seeming misinformation, lack human judgment, and had reached over 100 million users by early 2023. Its technology assessment notes generative AI's heavy water and electricity demands, citing International Energy Agency figures that U.S. data center electricity consumption was about 4 percent of demand in 2022 and could reach 6 percent by 2026. A report on machine learning in natural hazard forecasting describes a few operational models, data gaps in rural areas, trust and bias concerns, and five policy options. GAO's testimony describes its own deployment of a large language model and eight internal AI use cases, and notes nearly 50 AI products since 2018, 20 ongoing projects, and 35 recommendations to 19 agencies in December 2023.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: GAO reports that 20 of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, with about 200 in current use; five agencies gave comprehensive information for each use case while 15 had incomplete or inaccurate data; 10 of 23 agencies implemented all agency-specific AI requirements, 12 some and one was exempt; the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense AI research and development; generative AI reached over 100 million users by early 2023; U.S. data center electricity consumption was about 4 percent of demand in 2022 and could be 6 percent in 2026; GAO issued nearly 50 AI products since 2018 and made 35 recommendations to 19 agencies in December 2023; its 2021 accountability framework identifies 31 key practices.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone following AI in government, GAO is the closest thing to a public ledger. Its inventory review shows what agencies say they are running, how much of it is real versus planned, and where reporting breaks down, which is the starting point for oversight, budgeting and procurement questions. Its framework and recommendations give agencies a benchmark for responsible use, and its own internal deployment shows how a legislative branch agency is testing large language models under its own accountability practices. The technology assessments add the risk side, from hallucinations to energy and water use, that policymakers weighing expansion need to account for.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Government

sections.body: The material is audit and assessment work rather than operational data, so it reflects what agencies reported to GAO, which the reports themselves describe as sometimes incomplete, inaccurate or later corrected. Several findings are dated to specific reporting cycles, such as the January 2024 count of eight internal GAO use cases and the 2023 inventory review, and the policy landscape they describe may have moved since. The pages read do not cover classified or unreported AI uses, and the technology assessments explicitly note that private developers do not disclose some key technical information, which limits definitive statements about risk.
